title: Twenty-Two Seasons of Extremes, Finally Countable
summary: The AFL Record Book is live — highest scores, biggest blowouts, closest finishes, longest streaks and the most-played rivalries, drawn from all 5,333 games the league has ever played.
description: Here is a thing that was quietly impossible until this week: naming the biggest blowout in AFL history. MFL's archives had handed back 2007 through 2019 with the regular-season matchups stripped out, so any all-time list you built stopped being about the league and started being about whichever years happened to survive. Those seasons have now been pulled back in and checked against the official standings, and the Record Book is what you do with them.

It answers the questions that come up in the chat every year. The biggest blowout ever is Your Team Sucks over Joey's Team by 136.16 — in 2004, a season that was almost entirely invisible on this site until now. The closest finish is one hundredth of a point: The Mariachi Ninjas 110.77, The Boondock Saints 110.76, week 9 of 2015. The highest single game belongs to Drunk Indians, 231.72 in 2021. The longest winning streak is 16 straight by Whitman's Wonders, running from week 11 of 2011 into week 4 of 2012, and the longest losing streak is 16 as well, by Badd Boys, which took them from week 5 of 2015 to week 2 of 2016.

There are ten boards in total: highest single game, biggest blowout, closest finish, highest combined score, longest winning and losing streaks, most-played and most lopsided rivalries, best regular season and most points in a season. Every rivalry and every game links straight through to the pairing page, so you can go from "we got destroyed once" to the full series in one tap.

Two deliberate choices worth knowing about. Franchises appear under the name they carried that season — Cliffside Killer Clowns, Dicks out for Harambe, Taco Hell — because a record book that renames history is a worse record book. And forfeits are excluded: a 0.00 is not a performance, and letting them in would have handed "biggest blowout" to games nobody played.

One permanent hole, printed on the page rather than hidden: the AFL played its 2003 season on Yahoo and only the standings were ever typed into MFL. No game from that year has a score anywhere, so nothing from it can appear. Every season from 2004 on is complete.

title: The Pecking Order Comes to the AFL
summary: Claude Schefter's Tuesday-morning column now runs in the AFL too — all 24 franchises ranked 1 through 24, with trend arrows, five weekly awards, and a conference-by-conference standings snapshot. Half your all-play record, half your last three weeks, and not one ounce of credit for the schedule doing you a favor.
description: TheLeague has spent a season being told, every Tuesday morning, exactly where it stands. The AFL has spent that same season with 24 teams, two conferences, four divisions and no single page willing to say which of them is actually any good. That page exists now.

The math is the same argument it is on the other side of the site, and it is deliberately a short one. Half of your score is your all-play record — if you had played every team every week, how often would you have won? The other half is your last three weeks of scoring. Both halves are scaled against the field before they are added, so fifty-fifty means fifty-fifty. Your head-to-head record does not vote. That is the entire point: the column exists to look past the thing the standings already tell you.

In a 24-team league that distinction has teeth. Look at the Week 14 issue and Balls Deep sit second on a .638 all-play while riding a four-game losing streak, and Vitside Mafia jumped three spots on a 3-1 stretch that the standings barely register. Both of those are the formula arguing with the record, out loud, in public.

Underneath the rankings: Stat of the Week, Bench Blunder of the Week (the AFL leaves a genuinely upsetting number of points on the bench), Heater, Cooler, and next week's Matchup of the Week, picked as the highest-ranked clash on the slate. Then a standings snapshot split the way the AFL actually thinks — American League North and South, National League East and West — with the full 24-team all-play table beside it.

One AFL-specific wrinkle worth knowing: the league plays double-header weeks, and the column counts them honestly. The record beside each team covers the last three weeks it played, not the last three games, so a doubleheader shows up as "3-1 over their last 4" instead of quietly dropping a game on the floor.

Two issues are up now — 2025 Weeks 13 and 14 — so you can see the trend arrows working. From kickoff, a fresh one lands every Tuesday morning, and Schefter announces it in the chat with the top of the order and the week's worst bench decision.
imageAlt: The AFL Pecking Order Week 14 issue: Schefter's headline and lede above the 1-24 rankings, each card showing the team crest, a one-line verdict, and its all-play percentage, last-three-week PPG, season PPG and composite score.

title: The Pecking Order Stops Grading on Five Curves
summary: Two things decide the rankings now: your all-play record and your last three weeks. Fifty-fifty, and the team colors are finally readable in dark mode.
description: The Pecking Order used to blend five ingredients — recent form, head-to-head record, all-play percentage, season PPG and average margin — which sounds thorough and mostly meant nothing moved. Two of those five measure the same thing twice (season PPG and margin are both "you score a lot"), and head-to-head record is the one number the whole column exists to look past. Win a shootout by half a point and lose a 130-point week to the league leader, and the old formula quietly rewarded you for both.

It is now half your all-play record and half your last three weeks. All-play asks the only fair season-long question there is: if you played everybody every week, how often would you win? The rolling three-week scoring average asks the other one: are you any good right now? Nothing else votes. Season PPG and average margin still show on every card as context — they just do not move you anymore.

Both halves are scaled against the field before they are added, so fifty-fifty means fifty-fifty. On an absolute scale a league full of all-play numbers bunched between .300 and .700 would have quietly counted for about half as much as the scoring side, which is exactly the kind of thing that hides in a five-ingredient blend.

The visible effect: teams whose record is better than their football stop coasting, and teams getting beaten by the schedule stop being buried. In this week's issue Da Dangsters climb to #3 on a .710 all-play, and Wascawy Wabbits — a .659 all-play team scoring 93 a week lately — sit at #8, which is exactly the argument the two halves are supposed to have.

Separately, and long overdue: every team accent on the page was being rendered in the franchise's raw brand color, which is fine until dark mode. Bring The Pain is near-black and Cowboy Up is navy, so their rank numbers were effectively invisible on a dark card; in light mode Midwestside's yellow had the same problem against white. Every franchise color on the site now resolves to a version that stays readable on whatever theme you're in, brand-accurate where it already worked, nudged only where it did not.
imageAlt: The Pecking Order Week 17 rankings in dark mode, each card showing a readable team-colored rank number alongside the team's all-play percentage, last-three-week PPG, season PPG and composite score.

title: Roger Can Be Wrong. Now You Can Say So Without Deleting the Question.
summary: Every Ask Roger card gets a “This answer looks wrong” button. Report it, say why, and the commissioner sees it — the question stays right where it is.
description: Two of Roger's answers turned out to be wrong this month, and both took an embarrassingly long time to catch. The taxi squad ruling stood for seventeen days. The 5th-year option card had the wrong salary formula on it since March. In both cases somebody read the wrong answer, moved on, and nobody had a way to say anything.

That's because there wasn't one. The only lever on a bad answer was the commissioner's delete button, and deleting is a blunt instrument — it throws away the question along with the answer. The owner who asked it loses their card, their name comes off it, and the next person with the same question starts from scratch. So nothing got deleted, and wrong answers just sat there.

Now every card has a “This answer looks wrong” button. Hit it, optionally type what's actually wrong, and it's logged. The card picks up a red banner so the next owner scrolling past knows not to lean on it, and the commissioner sees who reported it and why. Changed your mind? Undo it. Nothing gets deleted, ever.

Worth knowing: this works on the pinned League Office cards too, not just the ones Roger writes on the fly. The 5th-year option mistake was on a hand-written card, which is exactly the kind nobody thinks to double-check. And a correction to the rulebook still doesn't rewrite an answer that's already on the page — Roger writes each one once and it stays written — so flagging it is what actually gets it looked at.
imageAlt: An Ask Roger card about the 5th-year team option showing a red banner reading “2 owners reported this answer as wrong — the commissioner is reviewing it”, the list of reporting teams and their reasons, and a “You reported this — undo” button.

title: Twenty-Three Years of Grudges, Finally Written Down
summary: AFL franchise pages now carry an all-time record, single-game highlights, a top-five rivals list and a full trade ledger — plus a brand-new rivalry matrix showing what every franchise has done to every other one since 2004.
description: The AFL franchise page has spent its whole life showing you a trophy wall and a name history and then just… stopping. No record. No points. No sense of whether this franchise has been good for twenty years or good for one. That page now opens with the numbers: all-time record, win percentage, seasons played, career points, points per game, playoff appearances. Smokane FC, for the record, is 232-157 across 23 seasons with 46,022 points. That is a lot of football nobody could see until today.

Underneath it: Single-Game Highlights. Your best day ever, your worst day ever, and the two blowouts — the one you handed out and the one you took. Then Top Rivals, which is the part worth arguing about. It ranks opponents on how charged the series actually is, not just how often you played: an even record counts for more than a lopsided one, and playoff meetings count triple. Smokane's list is led by Fullybaked — 14-9 across 23 games with seven playoff meetings, which is more postseason history than most franchises have with anyone.

Every rival links to a full pairing page: the whole series in one table, every meeting since 2004, with closest game, biggest blowout, highest combined score and longest winning streak on top. Those pages know what round each playoff game was, too — Quarterfinal, Semifinal, AL and NL Conference Championships, NIT Championship, the whole ladder. And there is now a Rivalry Matrix under Franchises, split by conference, where you can read one franchise's record against all eleven of its conference-mates in a single row and see the hot pairings shaded red.

Last piece: the Trade Ledger. Every deal this franchise has ever made, grouped by year, with what went out, what came back, and the trade comment the owner typed at the time. Each partner links straight to your rivalry page with them, because a trade history and a grudge history are the same history.

One caveat when this shipped, since resolved: MFL's archived exports returned 2007-2019 with the regular-season matchups stripped, so head-to-head totals under-counted badly and leaned toward playoff games — Smokane's rivalry pages covered 233 of its 389 career games. Those seasons have since been recovered from MFL's authenticated schedule view and verified against the official standings, so every AFL season from 2004 on is now complete: Smokane's pages carry all 462 of its meetings. The one permanent gap is 2003, which the league played on Yahoo with only standings entered into MFL — no game from that season has a score anywhere, so it is missing from every rivalry record and always will be.
imageAlt: The AFL Rivalry Matrix: a Hottest Rivalries strip of head-to-head cards showing each pairing's record, total meetings and playoff count, above a per-conference grid where every franchise's record against each conference rival is shaded by intensity.

title: The Audit Comes for TheLeague: 8 Division Banners Change Hands, and 2022 Comes Back From the Dead
summary: Same homebrew tiebreaker, same bad math — this time in TheLeague's record books. MFL's official standings are now the source of truth, eight division titles just moved, and an entire missing season got its wins back.
description: Fresh off auditing the AFL's record books, we pointed the same flashlight at TheLeague. Same rot. The code crowning each division winner sorted by raw division record FIRST, which is not a thing the constitution says anywhere. Read the rulebook: division record is tiebreaker number two. Overall record wins the division. What that bug produced was ten seasons where a team with a worse record got the banner because it happened to beat up on its own division — 2020 Eastern went to a 12-6 club over a 14-4 one, and the 2025 Northwest and Southwest were both handed to the runner-up. Eight of those ten are banners you can actually see change hands on a franchise page; the other two (2015 Central, 2018 Southwest) went to teams from an earlier ownership era, so nobody's page was showing them either way.

So we did what we did for the AFL: stopped re-deriving history and went to the source. MFL applies the constitution's full tiebreaker chain itself, and its official standings order now decides every division title. If you want the single case that settles the argument, it's 2015 Central. Amish Rakefighters and The Executioners both finished 15-3, both went 4-2 in the division. The Executioners scored more points AND had the better all-play record, so every version of our math picked them. MFL picked Amish — because Amish swept the season series, 120.66-91.19 in Week 1 and 136.34-127.01 in Week 3. Head-to-head. Step one. It's the one tiebreaker our code could never see, because the standings feed doesn't carry it.

Then there was 2022, which the record books had simply lost. MFL's export for that season ships the win-loss columns in a different shape, and our reader was looking for the wrong one — so every franchise in TheLeague was carrying a 0-0-0 for 2022 while somehow having scored two thousand points. No division titles, no wins, no losses, a whole year of football filed under nothing. It's back: Vitside Mafia's 15-3, Dark Magicians' 14-4, all four division winners, and roughly a hundred and forty games returned to career records across the league.

We also went looking for the titles nobody could claim. Twenty-five division championships were won under a previous owner of a franchise slot — Amish Rakefighters, LBer-DeCleaters, Acer FC Edge, the Sabertooths — and because career stats follow the human and not the jersey, those banners had nowhere to live and were silently dropped from the record entirely. They're now written down under the names that won them, which is the necessary first step; putting them somewhere you can actually look at them is a job for another day. Meanwhile every standings page in TheLeague renders MFL's official order, and a regression suite locks all of it down so no homebrew math ever crawls back into the record books.

title: Justice Is Served: Thundering Herd Is Dead, Long Live "A Bruin Pegs Me"
summary: Two titles, three conference crowns, and a proud dynasty — none of it matters when you finish dead last in the D-League. Franchise 0014 has been served its punitive rename, and the record books already know it.
description: The D-League doesn't grade on a curve, and it definitely doesn't care about your trophy case. Franchise 0014 — two-time champion, three-time NL conference king, the Herd desk's own nostalgia machine — bottomed out the standings this season, and the league's oldest tradition came for its name. Thundering Herd is retired. "A Bruin Pegs Me" is what's stitched on the jersey now.

The old name isn't erased, just filed where it belongs: the franchise page's history tab still remembers every era back to 2003, the current owner keeps every year of stats and hardware they earned along the way, and the site's search bar will still find you if you type "Herd" out of muscle memory.

And the paperwork has now caught up. The new crest and banner are live across the site — a UCLA cheerleader in powder blue and gold, bat in hand, which for an owner who bleeds cardinal and gold is the part that actually stings. The franchise's brand colors moved to navy and gold to match, so every roster row, matchup card and player headshot backdrop wears it too. Thirteen trophies, third-most in the league, all still on the wall above it.
imageAlt: The A Bruin Pegs Me franchise page showing the new UCLA-themed banner above the trophy wall and championship badges.

title: The Record Books Get an Audit: 22 Division Titles Restored to Their Rightful Owners
summary: Historical AFL division titles were being computed with a homebrew tiebreaker instead of the constitution. MFL's official standings are now the source of truth — and 22 banners just changed hands, from 2004 all the way to last season.
description: Somewhere along the way, the site's record books started freelancing. When we backfilled two decades of AFL history, the code crowning each division's champion sorted by division record first — and at one point even used raw points-for as a tiebreaker. That's not how this league works. The constitution is clear: overall record wins the division, and ties run the full gauntlet — head-to-head, division record, conference record, Power Rank, points, all-play, victory points, most points allowed, coin flip. MFL has been applying those exact rules all along.

So we stopped re-deriving history and went to the source. MFL's official final standings now decide every division title, every season, 2004 through 2025 — and an independent recomputation using the constitution's own tiebreaker chain agrees with MFL in all 100-plus division-seasons on the books. The fallout: 22 division banners moved to their rightful owners. Dicks out for Harambe's 12-5 season finally beats a 9-8 record for the 2025 AL South crown. Chatmaster's 14-3 masterpiece in 2017 takes the NL West it always deserved. And the all-time trophy count has a new king: the Drunk Indians, at 19 pieces of hardware, with Smokane FC sliding to second at 17.

The standings pages got the same treatment — historical and current standings now render in MFL's official order on every AFL surface, so the trophy room, the standings page, and the playoff picture finally tell the same story. A regression suite now locks all of this in so no homebrew math ever sneaks back into the record books.

title: The Keeper Report Card: Hindsight Is Undefeated
summary: A new Claude Schefter report grades every AFL keeper class by the only judge that matters — what actually happened. Your 2024 roster re-ranked by 2025 points, the seven you should have kept highlighted, and every hit, miss, and the-one-that-got-away called out by name. A keeper is worth the points he scored in the games you could have started him — backups count a fraction — so the grade is about the call you made, not the roster you inherited. Flip to 2026 to see this year's classes waiting for kickoff.
description: You had all offseason. You studied the roster, you agonized over the seventh spot, you declared your keepers with the quiet confidence of a person who has definitely not just protected a running back about to lose his job in training camp. And then the season happened. The Keeper Report Card is where those two stories meet: every franchise's previous-season roster, re-ranked by what those players scored the following year, with the hindsight-optimal seven highlighted in green.

Every keep gets a verdict. Keep a top-seven scorer? Hit. Keep someone who finished ninth on your own roster? Miss. Let a top-seven scorer walk back into the draft pool? That's the one that got away, and yes, it's labeled in yellow so everyone can see it. The league summary up top crowns the best keeper class, names the worst keeper decisions, and tallies the misses league-wide.

Here is the part that decides the table, and it's mercifully simple: a player is worth the points he scored in the games you could actually have started him. The optimal seven have to fit a real lineup — one QB, one kicker, one defense, and six from RB/WR/TE — because a third quarterback with nowhere to play isn't a keeper, he's a paperweight with a clipboard.

Every class is then scored on the share of its own ceiling it captured: the value your keepers delivered, divided by the value of the seven you could have kept. That grades the call instead of the collection — the ceiling swings roughly 2x from the league's thinnest roster to its deepest, and nobody chose the roster they inherited. Max out a thin roster and you'll beat a rival who left points on a loaded one.

Backups aren't written off — they're credited the share of their points they'd realistically have played. A seventh skill player rotates in across six flex starters' byes and matchups, so he counts 7/10 of his points. A second quarterback, kicker, or defense only plays the starter's bye week and the odd matchup call, so he counts 1/10. Both are “backups” and they are nowhere near equally valuable — bench keeps are marked Bench and priced accordingly.

Kickers and defenses aren't excluded from anything. Your starting kicker's points are real points at a real lineup slot, and passing on a big-leg season can be a genuine miss. A second kicker, though, counts a tenth of his points — which is the polite way of saying stop stockpiling kickers.

The bottom of the page spells out the whole rubric, because a report card that doesn't tell you how it grades is just a number with an attitude. The page defaults to the last finished season while we wait on kickoff. title: The AFL Franchise Page Finally Read Its Own Record Book
summary: The franchises page graduates from a name tag and a trophy count to the full career ledger — all-time records, seasons served, career points, and a rack of title pills for every club — sorted into proper American League and National League sections. Twenty-three years of receipts, one page.
description: For a league that has been settling scores since 2003, the AFL franchises page was strangely shy about it: an icon, a name, a division pill, and — if you'd actually won something — a lone trophy emoji doing all the talking. Meanwhile TheLeague's franchise page has spent months strutting around with career records and a badge shelf. The beat desk kept both tabs open and the comparison was not kind.

No longer. Every card now carries the club's all-time record with winning percentage, seasons served, and career points — computed from every standings feed back to 2003, and it follows owners across franchise moves the same way the trophy room does, so your record is yours, not the slot's. Below the numbers sits the full title rack: AFL Championships, Premier League crowns, conference and division flags, D-League titles, even the NIT — hover any pill for the years. The cards sort by hardware first, wins second, inside proper American League and National League sections, and each one glows in its team color when you reach for it. The icon stays — this is the AFL, we lead with the crest.

The Former Identities archive now sits in the open instead of behind a collapsed toggle, all several dozen punitive rebrands of it. title: The Footer Grew a Trophy Case
summary: Every page now ends on the defending champion — banner art, trophy badges, and a ribbon that knows the difference between a Double and a Treble — over a five-column directory that finally admits the whole site exists.
description: The old footer was four thin columns of links, two of which went to the same page, sitting next to a champion banner that only TheLeague ever saw. On AFL and Best Ball the layout quietly collapsed into a 300-pixel gutter and left half the footer empty. Nobody complained, because nobody scrolls down to be disappointed. Still. It was there, on every page, being wrong.

Now the bottom of every page opens with the champions. Full banner art, the trophy badges that team actually won, and a ribbon that counts: two titles is The Double, three is The Treble. title: AFL Free Agents: Your Conference, Your Board
summary: The free agent page now opens straight onto YOUR conference — every player listed is someone your team can actually add — with an AL/NL switcher in the header for scouting across the aisle. No more squinting at a guy the other conference already rosters.
description: The AFL runs two of everything — two conferences, two pennant races, and yes, two copies of every NFL player. Which made the old free agent page a bit of a bazaar: an American League owner would scroll past a shiny available tight end only to discover he was available in the National League. Technically true. Practically useless. The beat desk heard about it.

So the page now respects the aisle. Sign in and it opens on your conference — every name on the board is a player your team can genuinely add, and the counts, position pills, and the spotlight up top all agree with that math. A new switcher in the header flips the whole view to the other conference whenever you feel like scouting the neighbors, and the choice sticks in the URL so you can send a link that opens exactly where you left it.

Cross-conference intel didn't disappear — it just learned some manners. Tick Include rostered and players held in your conference show up dimmed, with an FA in NL (or AL) tag when the other side can still grab them. Combined with the live roster feed that landed alongside this — moves hit the page within about a minute of happening on MFL — the board finally answers the only question that matters: who can I add, right now?

title: Weekly Fixes & Polish (Jul 15-26)
summary: 19 bug fixes and style improvements across schefter report, rosters, draft, design system & theming, and more.
description: This week's 19 bug fixes and polish improvements touched the following areas of the site:

Schefter Report — Schefter's Cut Watch column got its facts straight about the August auto-cut. Sunday's article claimed the system cuts your weakest players when you skip filing a cutdown plan — flat wrong, and dangerously reassuring if your roster is loaded with recent pickups. The real rule: the machine cuts your NEWEST waiver, free-agent, and auction adds first, value be damned, and trades don't count as pickups. The shipped article was corrected, and future Cut Watch fact sheets now compute each team's actual auto-cut order with the exact code the deadline job runs — so when Schefter says the machine is coming for your quarterback, believe him. Schefter's daily Cut Watch dispatches were going straight to the website and skipping the group chat entirely — he'd type up 'Midwestside Connection faces the guillotine, 6 over the limit' for the site feed and then just... not hit send on GroupMe. Turns out the article pipeline only pings the chat for story types that define a promo, and Cut Watch never got one. Fixed: whenever at least one team is over the 22-man limit, the chat now gets the headline stat, how many players the league still needs to shed, the countdown to the August cutdown deadline, and a link to the full chopping block. On days when everyone's compliant, he keeps it to himself — no buzz for a non-story. And while we were in there, his editor dialed the column back from daily to a proper Sunday feature: one Cut Watch every Sunday morning of the cut window instead of thirty-three straight days of guillotine coverage. He also got a new source inside the league office: Schefter now knows which over-limit owners have already filed their auto-cut plans — those teams get a respectful nod for having their affairs in order, while the heat goes straight to anyone over the limit with nothing on file. He knows THAT you've made your picks, never WHICH picks — your cut list stays sealed. His chopping-block picks got smarter too: instead of just pointing at the cheapest contracts, likely cuts now come from a combined value ranking that blends redraft and dynasty ADP by contract length — a 1-year rental is judged purely on this season's draft boards, a 5-year keeper purely on dynasty boards. (Fixing that also uncovered that the 'dynasty ADP' feed had been a carbon copy of redraft data all along — now it actually pulls dynasty leagues.). The 'whisper back' links in Schefter's GroupMe posts work now. Every clean link on the league domains — afl-fantasy.com/schefter/tip, theleague.us/rosters, all of them — was quietly being stamped page-not-found behind the scenes; most pages shrugged it off and displayed anyway, but the tip page's sign-in handoff couldn't, so tapping a tip link from GroupMe dead-ended on a 404. The routing now reports what actually happened, the sign-in bounce goes through, and the link even remembers which team's desk you were headed to after you log in. Bonus: a bare /schefter now drops you at the Schefter Report feed instead of a dead end. Claude Schefter no longer ghosts you after one bad draft. When his quality gate spiked a post for being too vague, the scanner still charged it against the day's posting budget — so one scrapped rumor at 7am could silence the rumor mill until midnight, tips waiting patiently the whole time. Budgets now only count posts that actually ship. And when the feed's been quiet for a week (or a subject hasn't come up all week), the bar for 'worth posting' drops — a scrappy 3/10 rumor beats radio silence.

Rosters — The August cutdown automation now honors the rookie rule: before cutting anyone, it moves your rookies into open practice-squad spots — those players are KEPT, and every taxi move is one fewer cut. Premium draft picks get the spots first when you have more rookies than room, and marking a rookie in your cutdown plan still means what it says (he gets cut, not saved). The Cutdown Plan panel, the commissioner's report, and Schefter's Cut Watch all show the taxi moves now — green badges for the kept, amber for the doomed. The contract-action sheet caught up with the rest of the site's wardrobe. Open a player's contract tools on your phone and the headshot used to sit in a plain gray box — while every roster table around it dressed the same player in his team's colors. The modal now wears the standard player-cell chip: a circular team-color backdrop with the spotlight behind the head in dark mode, and a clean team-color ring in light mode. Same player, same colors, every surface. The Cut Watch reorder buttons were playing hide-and-seek in dark mode. The little up/down arrows and the × for un-marking a player were drawn in default-black ink on a near-black button — technically present, functionally invisible, especially on a phone where those arrows are the only way to reorder your cut list. The icons now inherit the button's actual color like every other icon on the site, so they show up crisp in both themes. The clipboard on the MARKED badge got the same treatment while we were in there. The roster loading screen learned to breathe. Its rotating one-liners were flipping every 2.2 seconds — just enough time to read half a quip before the next one shoved it offstage. Each line now hangs around for a full five seconds, and the loader itself waits a beat longer before appearing so quick page loads skip the theatrics entirely. The 'How It Works' tab clinging to the side of the Rosters page has been retired. It spent the spring walking newcomers through contract declarations, but with declaration season behind us it was just photobombing your roster — so the guided demo has left the building. The contract tools themselves haven't gone anywhere. The contract-year chips on the Rosters page — the little blue '4' with its ticking '27d' deadline badge — were still dressed for daylight in dark mode, glowing like sticky notes on a midnight desk. They now wear proper dark-mode colors: translucent fills, readable text, and a deadline badge that shifts from amber to orange to red as the clock runs down without searing your retinas on the way.

Draft — The draft room's player card was the last holdout on team colors. Tap a player in the draft room and the detail card popped up with his headshot floating in a plain gray circle with a position-colored ring — while the player list you just tapped him from had already dressed the same headshot in his NFL team's colors. The card now wears the standard player-cell chip: team-color gradient backdrop, spotlight behind the head, team-tinted ring in both themes. Bijan glows Falcons red on the card, same as he does in the list. Defenses keep their clean logo treatment. The Draft Order page now knows what phase of the calendar it lives in. During the season it's a live prediction that moves with the standings; once the champion is crowned and the toilet bowl comp picks are settled, it wears an official badge instead of hedging; and now that the rookie draft is in the books, it says so plainly — final order as drafted, with the next prediction cycle firing up when the new season kicks off. The spring draft heroes got the same memo and link to 'View Draft Order' instead of a predictor that stopped predicting months ago.

Design System & Theming — Light mode finally got the memo about team colors. The little circular player headshots have been wearing their NFL team's colors in dark mode for a while — gradient backdrop, soft spotlight behind the face — while light mode made do with a plain gray circle and a thin colored ring, like everyone showed up to the team photo in street clothes. No more: every player chip now wears the full team-color treatment in both themes, on every surface — rosters, player pools, free agents, live scoring, the contract sheet. The ring around each chip is cut from the same cloth, mixed darker in light mode so it frames the chip against a white page, lighter in dark mode so it pops off a black one. Bo Nix glows Broncos orange at noon and at midnight. The dark-mode player-headshot fix from earlier today found four stragglers. The live-scoring scoreboard was mixing its own paint — player chips built from raw team colors with none of the brightness safeguards, so a Titan or Steeler could still vanish into a midnight circle mid-game. The Projected Free Agents table and the AFL player pool had quietly skipped team colors entirely, showing plain gray chips in dark mode while their sibling pages got the full treatment. And the Rosters page's players-by-team and players-by-college cards were hand-sewing their own player rows without the backdrop. All four now use the same spotlight-behind-the-head backdrop as everywhere else, plus a half-opacity white ring that lifts every chip off the dark page. A new build-time guard makes it structural: any future page that hand-rolls its own team-color-behind-a-player math — or renders a player chip without the backdrop — fails the build and gets pointed at the shared helper. One paintbrush, whole site. Dark mode stopped hiding half the league's rookies. The little circular player headshots wear their NFL team's colors behind them — great in theory, except a third of the league (Titans, Steelers, Bears, Seahawks, Texans...) wears colors that are basically midnight, so a guy like Cam Ward in a navy jersey on a navy chip on a dark page was just a rumor of a face. The chips now reach for each team's lighter brand color when the main one is too dark — Titans light blue, Steelers gold, Bears orange — and every chip puts a soft spotlight right where the player's head sits, brightest behind the face and deepening toward the rim. Every team's backdrop is held to a minimum brightness, enforced by a build-time guard so no future team-color tweak can sink a headshot back into the void. Light mode untouched; it was never the problem. Dark mode got a full sweep of the closet. The Admin Hub bug from earlier this week — styling against color tokens that don't actually exist, so everything silently rendered its light-mode fallback — turned out to have cousins in some forty files: white draft-queue rows on a dark draft room, lineup accordions and matchup pickers stuck with light text, homepage urgency chips glowing like flashlights, and a templates page whose headings had no color at all. Every one now runs through the real theme tokens, and a new build-time guard fails any future code that references a token that doesn't exist — so this whole class of bug is done recurring.

Navigation & Routing — The side menu's league-switch chevron now actually switches leagues. On theleague.us and afl-fantasy.com it used to strip the other league's address right out of its own link — so 'Switch to AFL' just reloaded the page you were already on. It now carries you straight to the same page on the other league's site, and the chevron shows for everyone instead of hiding unless you were logged in as a dual-league owner.

Admin — The Admin Hub finally respects dark mode — its cards were stuck glowing white on the dark background because they styled themselves against token names that don't exist — and the August Cutdown Report now has a card there, so the commissioner's audit trail is one click away instead of a memorized URL.

Standings — Standings finally sit still on your phone — the Premier League tables (and every other standings view) used to shove the whole page sideways, so you had to swipe left and right just to read a record. Now the columns that matter — rank, team, and record — fit the screen, the rest tuck away until you've got the width for them, and the desktop layout is untouched.

title: Introducing Best Ball #1: Draft Once, Never Set a Lineup Again
summary: A third league joins the family — 12 teams, one 25-round startup draft run entirely on this site, and then absolutely nothing to manage. No waivers, no lineups, no trades. Draft well or wear it all season. The draft room is built, the mock lobby is open, and the clock is waiting.
description: Some leagues are marriages. TheLeague, with its contracts and cap sheets and August cut deadlines, is a marriage. Best Ball #1 is a first date that decides your entire year: one night, 25 rounds, 300 picks, and then you put the roster down and never touch it again. Your best scorers start themselves every week. That's the whole format. That's the whole league.

The main event runs right here on the site — the same live draft room engine that powers mock drafts, promoted to the real thing. Draft board, full veteran player pool sorted by redraft ADP (this is a win-now league; nobody's drafting for 2029), a pick queue, trash-talk chat, and an on-the-clock timer with an auto-pick safety net for whoever's getting a snack when their turn comes up. When the last pick lands, the results get imported to MyFantasyLeague and the season simply… runs.

Until draft night, the practice facility is open: the mock draft lobby spins up full 25-round rehearsals against the clock, and the Import Rankings page pulls your board in from FantasyPros or FootballGuys to power your queue. The rules fit on one page — which is the point. Draft once. Watch football. Argue about it in the chat. See you on the clock.
imageAlt: The Best Ball #1 league home: emerald hero announcing the 2026 startup draft with cards for the Draft Room, Draft Board, and Rosters.

title: The Cut List Is Now Yours to Boss Around
summary: Drag any player — even the machine's picks — into your cut order, unmark with one click, and watch a red dashed CUT LINE split who goes from who's safe. Oh, and the panel saves itself now, which beats its old habit of quietly forgetting your work.
description: First, a confession from the beat desk: until this week, the Cutdown Plan panel had a split personality. You'd mark your August cuts, watch the slate update beautifully — and then saving would post your original list and reset everything, like a waiter who nods through your whole order and brings you what the last table had. That bug is dead. And so is the Save button, because the panel now saves itself about a second after you stop fiddling — the status line tells you the moment your cuts are locked in, and it means it.

With the trust rebuilt, the slate got handed over to you completely. Every row is draggable now, not just your own picks — grab one of the machine's LAST ADDED selections, drop it where you want it, and it becomes YOUR PICK at that exact spot. On your phone, a Mark button does the same job with a tap, and every marked player wears an × so you can change your mind without opening his player card.

Best of all: marking more players than the deadline needs no longer hides the overflow. Everybody renders in one ordered list, split by a red dashed CUT LINE — players above it go on deadline night, players below it are your insurance, safe unless the roster grows. The numbering runs straight across the line, arrows and drags cross it freely, and even when you're at the limit with nothing to cut, your order stays visible and waiting. The automation still swings the axe. You just fully control the order of the chopping block.
imageAlt: The Cutdown Plan slate with three marked cuts above a red dashed cut line and a fourth marked player parked safely below it.

title: Your Roster Now Tells You Who's Getting Cut
summary: Over the 22-man limit? Your roster rows now wear the cut slate on their sleeves — gold AUTO-CUT badges in the exact order the deadline job will swing the axe. Mark nobody and it flags your newest pickups; mark your own and the badges flip to YOUR PICK.
description: Last month the Cutdown Plan panel promised the machine had your back at the deadline — "last players in are the first ones out." True, but abstract. A policy isn't a picture. Now it's a picture. Open your roster during the cut window and the players headed for the chopping block wear it right next to their name: a gold AUTO-CUT #1, #2, #3 badge, laid out in the exact order the automation will make the cuts.

Here's the part that matters: you don't have to mark a single player to see this. Marked nothing? The roster fills the slate with your most recent waiver and free-agent pickups and stamps each one LAST ADDED — because that's the tiebreaker the deadline job actually uses (and yes, players you traded for are safe; a deadline-week acquisition doesn't count as "just added"). Start marking your own casualties and those badges flip to YOUR PICK and jump to the front of the line. Same math, honest labels — AUTO-CUT for whoever's inside the cut line right now, MARKED for the insurance picks sitting safely below it.

A legend under the table does the accounting out loud — how many players are getting cut, and the night it happens — with a standing invitation to choose your own instead. Because the automation will happily pick for you. It's just picking by recency, not by heart. See exactly who's on the block, then go tell it who should be.
imageAlt: Roster rows during the August cut window with four players wearing gold AUTO-CUT #1 through #4 · LAST ADDED badges beside their contract years and salaries.

title: The AFL Rumor Mill Is Open: Tip Schefter Anonymously
summary: The beat desk's worst-kept secret weapon is now open for AFL business. Drop an anonymous tip — trade whispers, keeper intel, relegation panic, tampering chatter — and Schefter turns it into insider news. Nobody sees what you actually wrote. Not even the commish.
description: You know that thing where a rival GM leaks a story to the press just to watch another front office squirm? That's now a button on this website. The Schefter Rumor Mill — the anonymous tip line the beat desk has been running all offseason — is officially open for AFL business at Tip Schefter.

Here's the deal: you type the tip, Schefter's desk shreds the evidence. Your identity is one-way hashed before anything is stored, the raw text never gets printed, and only innuendo, rumor, and feeling survive the edit. You get a codename the moment you file — Burner Phone, The Ghost, Off the Record — and a spot on the tipster leaderboard when your intel makes the feed.

The topic list was rebuilt for how AFL front offices actually gossip: Trade interest. Keeper intentions ('hearing a team's letting a stud walk'). Relegation watch — because in this league, playing badly has consequences a spreadsheet can't hide. Tampering, for when somebody's been talking trade before the window opened. Front-office dysfunction, for everything else. Schefter marinates the queue, clusters corroborating whispers, and drops at most three rumors a day so every post hits.

One more thing, because the desk knows you'll ask: yes, there's a 60-second undo button now. Fat-thumb a tip, pull it back, no slot burned. The kitchen waits an hour before cooking anything, so your take-backs are safe. The tip line is live today — the AL and NL both have stories worth leaking, and Schefter has column inches to fill.
imageAlt: The AFL Tip Schefter page: anonymous tip form with topic and team selectors, Schefter's kitchen status, and the tipster leaderboard.

title: The Rumor Mill Learns Some New Tricks
summary: New NFL-insider topic lanes (hot seat, tampering, draft intentions), instant codename reveal, a 60-second undo, and in-form whisper-backs — the tip line just got a front-office upgrade in both leagues.
description: The tip form's topic menu graduated from message-board categories to actual insider beats: Hot seat, Tampering, Draft intentions, Front-office dysfunction, and Contract-year motives join the classics. Each one comes with its own editorial rules — tampering posts always hedge (an accusation is not a report), and hot-seat chatter never names a team, because you can all read a standings page and Schefter isn't doing the triangulation for you.

Quality-of-life, since you asked (loudly, anonymously): your codename is revealed the moment you file your first tip instead of whenever your first rumor prints. A 60-second undo pulls back a fat-thumbed tip with a full slot refund. And the form can now whisper back on any rumor from the last two weeks — pick the storyline, add your intel, and Schefter threads it.
imageAlt: The upgraded tip form showing the expanded topic list and whisper-back picker.

title: Cutdown Day Runs Itself Now
summary: Mark your August cuts from the player menu, let the new Cutdown Plan panel do the cap math, and sleep through the deadline — the automation executes your exact list at 8:45 PM PT so nobody has to set an alarm for roster panic.
description: Every August it's the same movie: the roster limit says 22, your roster says 25, and somewhere around 8:40 PM on deadline Sunday you're squinting at salaries on your phone trying to remember who you promised yourself you'd cut back in June. This year the movie has a different ending. Open the ⋯ menu next to any player on your roster and there's a new option — Mark for August auto-cut — and just like that, cutdown day stops being an appointment and starts being a decision you already made.

The brains live on the Rosters page in the new Cutdown Plan panel, which shows you exactly what deadline night will do to your roster — not roughly, exactly. Your marked players line up first, in your order, and if you're still over the limit the panel fills the rest with your most recent waiver and free-agent pickups, each row showing salary, dead cap, and net savings, with the total cap damage tallied underneath. Roster rows wear honest badges — AUTO-CUT for players inside the cut line, MARKED for insurance picks below it — and every number comes from the same math the deadline job runs, so the preview can't lie to you. Hit Save cut list, confirm your MFL login once, and the panel stamps your plan credentials-verified. Feeling decisive? Cut marked players now does it on the spot instead.

And if you do absolutely nothing? The automation still has you covered at the deadline — last players in are the first ones out, with one civilized exception: players you traded for don't count as "just added," so nobody's prized deadline-week acquisition gets swept out with the waiver-wire flotsam. Save a list, cut now, or let the machine sort it out — three ways to make the deadline, zero of them involving an 8:44 PM heart rate spike. The Cut Watch countdown on the homepage will still try to scare you. Now you can smile back at it.
imageAlt: The Cutdown Plan panel on the Rosters page showing three auto-selected cuts in execution order, each with salary, dead cap, and net savings, plus the Save cut list and Cut marked players now buttons

title: The Gauntlet: Schefter Ranks Every Team’s Road Ahead
summary: Claude Schefter’s new weekly column ranks every franchise’s remaining schedule from cupcake run to buzz saw — with a full dashboard, a week-by-week heat map, and receipts for whose record is lying.
description: Your record says 5-2. Congratulations. Now answer the uncomfortable question: 5-2 against WHOM? Starting this season, Claude Schefter answers it for you every Wednesday morning with The Gauntlet — his new schedule-strength column that rates every team’s remaining opponents on a 0-100 difficulty scale and ranks the league from “walking into a wood chipper” down to “booked a cruise through the soft part of the schedule.” Both leagues get their own edition, and yes, he built the model himself, and yes, he trusts it more than he trusts you.

The column is just the headline act. Behind it sits a full Schedule Strength dashboard: “The Run-In” ranks who has the hardest road left (with week-over-week trend arrows, because your schedule can get scarier while you sleep), “What They’ve Been Through” scores the slate each team has already survived, and the Schedule Luck callouts name names — the 6-1 team that’s been feasting on cupcakes, and the 1-6 team that’s secretly been playing murderers’ row. Scroll down for the week-by-week heat map: every franchise, every remaining week, color-coded green to red, each cell one click from your future opponent’s franchise page. Trap Weeks flags the Sunday the whole league hits a wall at once.

Every Wednesday the numbers recompute from settled stats, Schefter files his column to the Schefter Report, and one perfectly-calibrated teaser lands in the GroupMe — just enough to start an argument by lunch. Find Schedule Strength in site search, or wait for Wednesday and let the man tell you himself. Your record has an asterisk now. He put it there.
imageAlt: The Gauntlet schedule-strength dashboard showing the Week 9 run-in rankings with difficulty bars for every franchise

summary: Claude Schefter’s new weekly schedule-strength column now covers all 24 AFL squads — who has the cushiest run-in, who’s walking into a buzz saw, and whose record is a work of fiction.

The dashboard behind the column does the heavy lifting: “The Run-In” ranks who has the hardest road left with week-over-week trend arrows, “What They’ve Been Through” scores the slate each team already survived, and the Schedule Luck callouts name the 14-3 team that’s been feasting on the soft part of the fixture list. The week-by-week heat map paints every franchise’s remaining schedule green to red — one click from any cell to your future opponent’s trophy wall. Trap Weeks flags the Sunday the whole league hits a wall at once.

Fresh numbers recompute from settled stats every Wednesday morning, the column files to the Schefter Report, and one perfectly-calibrated teaser lands in the GroupMe. Relegation-zone teams checking whether the math offers any hope: it’s all there. It may not.

title: The Trade Block Comes to the AFL Trade Builder
summary: Players flagged on the trade block now show up right inside the AFL Trade Builder — see who is shopping, then start the trade in one click.
description: The AFL Trade Builder knew your roster, knew their roster, and knew exactly how lopsided your offer was. What it didn't know was who actually wanted to make a deal — you were cold-calling every roster in the conference like a telemarketer with a draft-pick script. That changes today: every player an owner has flagged on the trade block now headlines the Trade Builder in a new On the Trade Block panel, grouped by team, ranked by ADP.

See a player you like? Click him. If he plays for a conference rival, the builder loads that team and drops him straight into the 'They give' column — you're one counter-offer away from a done deal. Your own flagged players get the same treatment on your side of the ledger, and the little 🏷️ tag follows flagged players into the roster pickers and the team dropdown, so availability is visible everywhere you build. Teams from the other conference still show up on the block, but they're politely grayed out — cross-conference trades remain illegal, no matter how nicely you ask.

And yes, the block is now properly attributed: with both conferences drafting from the same NFL player pool, the old data couldn't tell WHICH team had flagged a player. Now it can. Flag a player from the Rosters page (the ⋯ menu next to any player) and the whole league knows you're open for business — the right you, on the right team.
imageAlt: AFL Trade Builder showing the On the Trade Block panel with flagged players grouped by team

title: Weekly Fixes & Polish (Jul 6-10)
summary: 21 bug fixes and style improvements across free agents, rosters, design system & theming, other, and more.
description: This week's 21 bug fixes and polish improvements touched the following areas of the site:

Free Agents — Player avatars in light mode got a lot less gloomy. The little circular headshots on the Free Agents list (and everywhere else the player lockup shows up) used to sit on a dark team-color gradient no matter the theme — heavy and hard to read against a bright white page. Light mode now uses a soft gray chip with a thin team-color ring instead; dark mode keeps its original moody gradient look untouched. Team defenses finally have a face in the free-agent pool. Tap a D/ST and, instead of a lonely logo staring back, the player card now leads with the unit's headliner — the Raiders' Maxx Crosby, say — his headshot on the team-color gradient and his name in the byline. It's the same trick the Free Agents spotlight already pulls up top, now brought into the detail card so a defense reads like the roster of real humans it actually is. The Free Agents hero stopped reaching for the shoebox photo. When the spotlighted player had no ESPN headshot, the panel used to fall back to a tiny, grainy MyFantasyLeague mugshot (or a gray "no photo" placeholder) — a blurry face is worse than none up in the hero. Now it simply hides the cutout and lets the team logo carry the panel, so the spotlight only ever shows a crisp headshot or a clean crest. Both The League and AFL boards get the fix.

Rosters — Fixed a cropped team logo on the Rosters page's Cap Hits / Dead Money table. The "[Year] Dead Money" total row shows a franchise crest instead of a player photo, but it was getting squeezed and cropped by the same circular-cutout treatment built for headshots — top of the logo clipped off. It now renders full and uncropped, just like the DEF logo chips elsewhere on the site. The "Step 1 of…" tracker at the top of the contract declaration flow stopped mumbling in the dark. That little progress label had been rendered in a dim gray that all but disappeared against the modal's dark backdrop, leaving you squinting to tell which step you were on. Bumped it to a brighter, theme-aware tone that reads cleanly in both light and dark mode — same understated label, now actually legible.

Design System & Theming — The Pacific Pigskins and Vitside Mafia crests finally got dark-mode variants. Both teams' logos used to stay stuck in their light-theme colors when you had dark mode on, standing out (in a bad way) against every other team's icon smoothly swapping over — now they blend in like everyone else, on both TheLeague and AFL sites. Team logos now dress for the dark. Marks with black outlines — the Raiders shield, the Steelers hypocycloids, the Jets, North Carolina's navy interlock — used to all but vanish against a dark background, a smudge where a logo should be. In dark mode every NFL logo across the site (matchup heroes, the composite banners, roster player rows) now swaps to its dark-optimized cut, outline flipped to white so the crest actually reads, and the college logos in the Free Agents and roster player tables get the same treatment. Light mode is untouched, and the switch follows your theme toggle in real time. The Schefter Ops dashboard finally turned the lights off. In dark mode the commissioner's rumor-mill control room had been stranded in daylight — every card stayed stark white while the page around it went dark, and the text painted on top all but vanished into the glare. Wired the whole page into the real dark theme so cards, borders, code chips and status text all dim down properly. Commish-only, so nobody else ever saw the flashbang. The "Back to MFL" strip up top got a smoother fade in dark mode. That deep-blue glow band was cutting off to fully transparent partway up, leaving a visible seam where it met the near-black page. Tuned the gradient to fade out at a soft trailing tint instead of hard zero, so the strip blends into the page instead of stopping short.

Other — Live Scoring no longer sits empty in the offseason. With the NFL season over, MyFantasyLeague switches its live feed off — so out of season, tapping Live Scoring in the nav dropped you on a barren "Scores will appear here when games begin" screen. Now, whenever the feed's dark, the page plays back the last completed regular season's final week as if it were unfolding live: real starting lineups built from the actual box score, some matchups final and others mid-play with live win-probability bars, game clocks, and projected finals that land on the real results — all flagged with a "Sample data" badge so nobody mistakes it for a live game. The instant the season kicks off and the feed lights back up, it flips to real-time scores on its own — no toggle, no special link. Live Scoring's matchup detail finally shows both rosters on a phone. Tap into a matchup and scroll to the player-by-player breakdown: your lineup sat on the left, the numbers ran across the middle, and the opponent's entire starting nine spilled clean off the right edge — you couldn't see the team you were playing without a sideways swipe. Rebuilt the row for small screens so both sides fit at once: your player on the left, theirs on the right, each tagged with its own color-coded position chip and score, real headshots on both. Long names now tuck to an ellipsis instead of bulldozing the score beside them, and nothing runs past the screen. The desktop layout — full names, team and game clock, projections — is untouched. The Live Scoring scoreboard stopped running out of bounds on phones. Tap into a matchup on your phone and the big score-header — two teams, their crests, and those jumbo live totals — had been spilling off the right edge, shoving the home team's score clean off-screen behind a phantom horizontal scroll. Reworked it so each side stacks tidily (crest and name up top, the giant number underneath) and the whole card now fits the screen with everyone visible. While we were in there, the "← All matchups" back button got a little breathing room above the scorecard instead of sitting right on top of it. Claude Schefter is back on the beat. His scanner — the one that breaks transaction news and fires Roger's event reminders — had quietly flatlined: a duplicate line snuck into its scheduler config, which is the kind of typo the robots refuse to forgive, so the whole job got rejected before it ever woke up. Every run since had failed silently. Cleared the duplicate and the newsdesk is live again. Live Scoring stopped hiding the fine print after dark. When a player was booming — matching or beating his projection — his cell lights up with a green wash, but in dark mode the little "proj" number tucked underneath stayed a dim gray that all but dissolved into that glow, so the one line telling you what he was supposed to score went unreadable right when it mattered. Tinted it a legible mint that sits cleanly on the green in dark mode (and a deep green in light), so the projection reads at a glance whether or not the player's on a heater.

Homepage — What's New finally moved into the AFL homepage. The League has had that little row of recent-update cards on its front page for a while; now AFL owners get the same feed on afl-fantasy.com, browser-frame screenshots and all, pointed at the right domain. While we were in there the whole card treatment got a glow-up on both sites: the category accent colors — the little stripe and pill on each card — were a muddy, muted set that barely registered, so they got brightened to punchier greens, blues, violets and reds, and they now light up even bolder in dark mode instead of sulking. The cards themselves stopped floating shapeless against the page and picked up the same proper border and drop-shadow depth every other card on the site already wears, in both light and dark. The "Completed auctions report" link on the homepage auctions card now stays in one piece. It had been breaking mid-phrase — "Completed" clinging to the end of one line while "auctions report" dropped to the next — so the whole link now wraps to a fresh line together when it runs out of room. The homepage and season heroes stopped whispering in daylight. In light mode the whole family — the What's New announcement, the weekly recap, the waiver and weekend-preview articles, the auction and cut-watch panels, the champion-crowned card, the AFL event hero and more — had faded to pale, near-white washes that all but vanished against the page, hoarding every bit of drama for dark mode. Now each wears a bold saturated card in every theme, keyed to its own color: deep league-blue for most, warm amber for the auction, alarm-red for breaking news and roster cuts, trophy-gold for a champion crowned. White headlines, on-brand glow, and the featured player bigger than ever — the daylight version finally hits as hard as the night one. The player on the Cut Watch hero got a growth spurt. The bubble-player cutout — the face staring back at you while the roster-deadline countdown ticks — was sitting a little small in the corner, so we sized him up to fill the frame the way he was always meant to. More presence, same panic. Mobile is untouched. The Cut Watch bubble player scooted over to claim the wall. He'd been floating a couple dozen pixels shy of the hero's right edge, leaving an awkward sliver of empty gradient between his shoulder and the frame. Now he's pinned flush to the edge where he belongs — same panic-inducing stare down the roster-deadline countdown, just anchored properly instead of drifting. Mobile is untouched.

site — Wander off the map and you no longer hit a broken-looking dead end. The old 404 page had two lines of text hard-coded to near-black, so in dark mode "Page Not Found" all but disappeared into the void. The whole page got rebuilt as a Claude Schefter breaking-news alert instead: a red BREAKING banner, Schefter's mugshot on the byline, a giant 404, the headline "Sources say this page doesn't exist," and a LIVE ticker scrolling league-flavored bulletins along the bottom ("Developing: URL reportedly entered the transfer portal"). Reads perfectly in both light and dark now, and instead of making you pick a league, a single button — labeled "Back to AFL" on afl-fantasy.com and "Back to The League" on theleague.us — drops you on the homepage of whichever site you wandered off of.

Live Scoring — Live Scoring's win-probability bars finally show their true colors after dark. A bunch of teams carry near-black or deep-navy brand colors — Music City, the Magicians, Cowboy Up — and in dark mode those bars had been vanishing into the card or getting nudged to a muddy compromise, so you couldn't tell whose slice was whose. Every franchise now has a hand-picked dark-mode primary and secondary: Music City lights up in Titans sky-blue, the Magicians in bright Dark-Magician purple, and the rest in vivid, on-brand hues that read cleanly against the dark scoreboard. Light mode is untouched.

title: Throwback Week: The Old Names Ride Again
summary: Every Week 4, the league's weekly pages dust off the archives. Live scoring, matchups, and submit lineup swap every team's name, logo, banner — and colors — for a legacy identity from the franchise's own history. Thirty-seven eras of recovered art, from the Sabertooths to the skull wabbit. One week a season, the scoreboard becomes a family photo album.
description: Sixteen franchises, nearly two decades of rebrands, and a commissioner who spent a weekend spelunking the Wayback Machine so none of it stays buried. Every season, for Week 4 only, the weekly pages — live scoring, the matchup scoreboard, and submit lineup — roll every team back to an old identity. Old name, old logo, old banner, and yes, old colors: the matchup washes and win-probability bars tint in each era's own palette, sampled from the era's own art. Thirty-seven eras made the cut, every one wearing genuine recovered artwork — Degenerates green, Sabertooths orange, the Barney Fife bullseye.

Each team defaults to a commissioner-picked former self — Heavy Chevy gives way to the Drunk Indians, the Computer Jocks take the floor as the Witch City Warlocks, and Maverick puckers up as the 2012 'smooch' Poker in the Rear. Rather choose your own ghost? Throwback Settings lets every owner browse their franchise's eligible eras — same-name eras get their own nicknames ('The razorback', 'The skull', 'Red graffiti era') so you always know which vintage you're buying. Hit Preview on any era to see it live on the scoreboard before committing, then save it right from the preview when it looks right. Your pick sticks for every future Throwback Week until you change it.

The rest of the site keeps its head: standings, rosters, and the trade builder stay on current identities, so nobody's wondering who the Sabertooths are in the middle of a trade negotiation. (Only one team can be the Sabertooths anyway — we checked. It's the Geeks.) Then Week 5 arrives, everyone snaps back to the present, and the archives go back to sleep for another year. See you next September, Warlocks.
imageAlt: The live scoring scoreboard during Throwback Week, with matchup cards showing legacy franchise identities — old team names, logos, and banners from each franchise's history.

title: Set Contract Years Without Leaving the Homepage
summary: The Unsigned FA Adds card used to just point a finger at your default 1-year deals and send you off to Manage Contracts to actually do something about it. Now it does something about it right there.
description: The homepage has always been good at telling on you — 'hey, this pickup is still sitting on the default 1-year contract' — but it never let you fix it without a detour. Click through, find the player again, declare the years, hope you remembered the deadline. Small tax, paid every single time.

Tax repealed. Every eligible pickup on the card now has a Set years button that opens the same contract declaration flow the roster page uses — pick a term, hit declare, done, all without the card ever losing your place. And the card got smarter about who it shows: any player still inside the 48-hour (or 24-hour in-season) window now shows up, even after you've already declared — they just slide into a quieter Declared section with a status pill and a Change years button, in case you change your mind before the window closes.
Once the clock runs out, they age off the list either way — declared or not. The homepage was already the first thing you saw every visit; now it's also a place you can actually finish something.
imageAlt: The homepage Unsigned FA Adds card showing a player pickup with a 'Set years' button, and a contract declaration modal open with year-length options and a Declare Contract button.

title: What's New, Right on the Homepage
summary: You shouldn't have to go hunting to learn what changed. The two latest updates now ride at the bottom of the homepage's left column — a quick glance at what shipped while you were off tinkering with your lineup, no detour required.
description: For a while now the full What's New archive has lived a click away on its own page — perfect for a deep dive, a little much for a quick 'wait, what's different?' glance. So we brought the highlights home.

The two newest updates now sit at the bottom of the homepage's left column, just beneath Explore — each a tappable card with its headline, date, and a one-line pitch. 'All releases →' still takes you to the full history whenever you want the director's cut. And if a story's already headlining the hero up top, the panel quietly steps aside and shows the next one down, so you never read the same news twice on one screen.
It's a small thing that does a big thing: the stuff we ship stops being a secret you have to look up. Glance down, see what's new, get back to your roster.
imageAlt: The bottom of the homepage's left column showing a 'What's New' panel with two update cards side by side — each with a category badge, headline, date, and short summary — above an 'All releases' link.

title: Live Scoring Comes Home
summary: The Sunday scoreboard used to live on MyFantasyLeague's servers, in a gray grid of numbers with all the drama of a spreadsheet. No more. Live Scoring is now ours — every matchup, every point, projected finals and win probability, updating through the Thursday, Sunday, and Monday windows and dressed in your team's colors.
description: For years, checking who was winning meant bouncing out to the old MFL live-scoring page — a table that looked drawn in 2009. We rebuilt it from scratch, on our own turf, and gave it the broadcast treatment it always deserved.

The scoreboard floats the closest games to the top and pins your matchup up top in a card washed in both franchises' colors. Every matchup carries a live score, a projected final, and a win-probability bar that swings as your guys score — because 'you're up 12' and 'you're up 12 with their whole backfield yet to play' are very different Sundays.

Tap any matchup for the full head-to-head: starter by starter, live points over projection, each player's NFL team logo and live game state — green for on the field, amber for yet to play, a quiet gray once he's done. Beat your projection and the number lights up. The score header stays pinned while you scroll, so you never lose sight of the damage. It refreshes every 60 seconds through game windows, and yes — it was built for late nights, with a proper dark mode.
imageAlt: The Live Scoring scoreboard in dark mode: a featured 'Your Matchup' card washed from red to purple with the Pigskins and Magicians crests, live scores 64.3 and 76.9, projected finals, and a red-and-purple win-probability bar, above two smaller matchup cards.

title: AFL Free Agents, In-House
summary: A dedicated free-agent board — browse, sort, and filter every available player without leaving for MFL.
description: The Free Agents button in the header used to bounce you out to MFL's bare add/drop screen. Now it lands on a proper scouting board built right here — every available player laid out in one sortable, filterable table, with the top name of whatever you're looking at spotlighted broadcast-style up top.

Sort by projected points, dynasty ADP, or last season's total; filter by NFL team, age, height, weight, experience, and draft round; and tap the position pills to jump straight to the QBs, backs, receivers, tight ends, kickers, or team defenses on the market. Flip on "Include rostered" or "Include rookies" when you want the full pool. Click any name for the full player card.

It's a leaner cousin of the board the other league runs — no cap, contract, salary, or auction columns, because this is a keeper league that redrafts every offseason. Just the numbers that help you decide who to chase.
